title: Indra's Plea at Dwaraka
story:
The wind that afternoon carried a fragrance no garden of Dwaraka had ever produced, and flowers fell from a sky that had been clear a moment before. In the great assembly hall called Dasharha — whose golden doors opened onto a courtyard a full yojana across — the leading Yadavas sat at their daily business. Then a great noise filled the air, and through a net of light they saw the king of the gods descending on his white elephant Airavata, the celestials gathered about him.

Rama and Krishna went out at once, with King Ugrasena and the chiefs of the Vrishni and Andhaka houses, to receive him. Indra came down from the elephant, embraced Krishna and Balarama and the king in order of age and rank, and, honored by both brothers, entered the hall and accepted the offerings of hospitality. When he was seated, he reached out and touched Krishna's face with his hand — the auspicious countenance of his younger brother, as the old telling has it — and he spoke.

"By you, Madhusudana," said Indra, "the world's oppressors have fallen one by one — Arishta, Dhenuka, Chanura, Mushtika, Kesin, Kamsa, Kuvalayapida, and the child-killer Putana. By your valor the three worlds are preserved, and the gods receive their share of the sacrifices. But hear now why I have come. The demon Naraka, son of the Earth, king of Pragjyotisha, has grown swollen with a boon granted him by Brahma. He has stolen the earrings of my mother Aditi, which drip nectar. He has taken Varuna's umbrella, which no water can wet, and the jewel-crest of Mount Mandara. He has carried off the maidens of gods, saints, demons, and kings — sixteen thousand and a hundred of them, wearing a single braid — and shut them in a house he built for them on Mount Mani. And now, O Govinda, he demands my elephant Airavata."

The hall was silent. Indra went on: "He is unslayable by any creature — but not by you, O Upendra. Garuda will bear you to his city. Slay the sinful wretch, and come back."

Krishna smiled gently. He rose from his throne, took Indra by the hand, and thought of Garuda; and the great bird, who could range anywhere and take on any strength, was there in the courtyard. Krishna seated Satyabhama on his back, mounted behind her, and rose into the sky, turning east toward Pragjyotisha, where razor-edged nooses defended the demon's walls and four terrible guardians — Hayagriva, Nisunda, Panchanada, and Muru with his thousand sons — kept watch. Indra mounted Airavata and, in the sight of all Dwaraka, returned to the abode of the gods.

The city stood looking after them: the lord of Dwaraka flying out to war with his queen at his back, against a demon who had robbed the mother of the gods — and who would soon learn that Brahma's boon had a limit.
reflection: The king of the gods does not come to Dwaraka as a commander but as a supplicant, listing the oppressors Krishna has already removed and then naming the one he cannot. Indra's visit makes plain what the Yadavas have always suspected: their city is where heaven itself sends its hardest battles.
next_story_tease: But before the demon's fall, a quiet gift at a mountain festival would stir a storm in Krishna's own household.
hero_scene: Krishna and Satyabhama rising into the sky on Garuda's back above the assembly hall of Dwaraka, while Indra on his white elephant Airavata watches and the city gazes up.
